title: Fringe players on political Twitter: Source-sharing dynamics, partisanship and problematic actors
screen_reason: Behavioural Twitter study of link-sharing in political/issue keyword spaces around the 2020 U.S. election. It reports the share of all shared news sources that were labelled 'problematic' (inaccurate, misleading, inappropriately attributed or fabricated) by an expert source list built from AllSides, Media Bias/Fact Check, 'the Chart' and NewsGuard: 16% in March 2020, 30% in December 2020/January 2021, 11% in March 2021. That is a share of shared links carrying unreliable sources with a stated (if only approximate) denominator, i.e. SHARING (content_share) per §3's rule that '% of shared links unreliable' is SHARING, not CONTENT.

estimates.country: U.S. (2020 U.S. presidential elections; 'political Twitter' keyword/hashtag spaces for U.S. parties, candidates and social issues)
estimates.date: March 2-22, 2020 (representative period; the study also covers December 24, 2020-January 4, 2021 and March 10-22, 2021)
estimates.measure_type: % of all news-source links shared in political-Twitter keyword datasets that came from sources labelled problematic
estimates.value_raw: 16% of all shared news sources (March 2020); the other two waves: 30% (December 2020/January 2021) and 11% (March 2021)
estimates.denominator: All news-source links shared in tweets/retweets captured by the political and issue keyword/hashtag queries (Table 5.1: Democrat, Republican, Biden, Trump, DACA, Green New Deal, Medicare); the per-period denominator is not reported - 'around a million links to media articles were shared' across the three time frames, from 'close to 3 million tweets ... that contain a link to a news article'
estimates.definition: Each shared link's host was matched against an expert source list in which every source was labelled either mainstream or problematic (mainstream sources further sub-labelled (hyper)partisan conservative, (hyper)partisan progressive or neither); the numerator is the total number of TIMES problematic-labelled sources were shared
estimates.misinfo_def: "Problematic sources refer to Jack's characterization as containing information that is 'inaccurate, misleading, inappropriately attributed, or altogether fabricated' (2017, p. 1)."
estimates.n: not reported per period; ~1,000,000 shared links to media articles across the three time frames (Findings), from close to 3 million tweets containing a news link (Methods)
estimates.source_quote: In March 2020, the share of problematic news sources shared on Twitter was 16% of all shared news sources. In December, the share of problematic news sources almost doubled to 30%. In March 2021, the share of problematic sources dropped significantly to 11%.
estimates.page_loc: Findings, Finding 1, pp. 92-93 (also Essay summary, p. 84, and Figure 5.1)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors' own 'expert list' of news sources, compiled from existing labelling sites - Allsides.com, Media Bias/Fact Check, 'the Chart' and NewsGuard - into two main categories (mainstream / problematic) plus (hyper)partisan sub-labels; the authors state 'We consider the categorization as rough.' No inter-coder reliability for the source list; the list itself is not reproduced in the chapter (data at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/QIJQ3X).
estimates.moderator_quote: To study the most shared links, an expert list of sources was created. Each source was labeled into two main categories, mainstream or problematic. Mainstream sources could be sub-categorized as (hyper)partisan conservative, (hyper)partisan progressive or neither. The expert list was created using existing labeling sites such as Allsides.com, Media Bias/Fact Check, "the Chart," and NewsGuard. We consider the categorization as rough. By calculating the total number of times problematic sources were shared during our duration of study and comparing it with the mainstream sources we were able to show the magnitude of the matter at hand.
estimates.notes: TIME SERIES COLLAPSED to one representative point per instruction §2. The three waves give 16% (March 2-22, 2020), 30% (December 24, 2020-January 4, 2021) and 11% (March 10-22, 2021). I chose March 2020 as representative because it is the earliest and longest window (3 weeks vs ~12 days), it precedes both the election and Twitter's January 2021 purge of 70,000+ accounts, and it happens to be the median of the three values. An adjudicator wanting the post-election peak should use 30%, or 11% for the post-purge period. Note the paper's own inconsistency: the Essay summary gives the third wave as 'just over 10%' while Finding 1 gives 11%. Denominator caveat: no per-period link count is published, and the ~1 million (Findings) vs ~3 million tweets with news links (Methods) figures cannot be reconciled from the text, so the denominator size is approximate - hence confidence medium. Note also that the third wave was collected with different software (4CAT rather than DMI-TCAT), which the chapter does not treat as a comparability problem.

missed_or_uncertain: Deliberately not extracted: (1) The (hyper)partisan share - 'The percentage of mainstream sources shared from sources subcategorized as (hyper)partisan decreased slightly from 48% in March 2020 to 43% in December and further dropped to 33% in March 2021' (Essay summary says 'a drop to 34%' for 2021, contradicting Finding 1's 33%). No row, for two reasons: its denominator is MAINSTREAM shares only, not all shares, so it is not comparable with the 16%/30%/11% series; and the authors explicitly place (hyper)partisan outside the problematic category - 'While (hyper)partisan sources do not share conspiracy or pseudo-science and are not problematic in that sense'. Combining the two categories into a broader 'problematic or hyperpartisan' share would be a cross-category sum, forbidden by R8. An adjudicator who counts hyperpartisan sources as 'unreliable/junk' would add a definition_variant row with value 48 (March 2020), denominator = mainstream shares. (2) Problematic ACCOUNTS - 'In our datasets in total, problematic accounts in January make up about 60% of all accounts which is roughly the same as in March' (Finding 4). This is a share of the top-20 most-active accounts classified as fake, bot or locked/suspended, i.e. account INAUTHENTICITY, not a share of misinformation content, shares or exposure; the denominator ('our datasets in total' - top 20 users across the Democrat, Republican, Biden and Trump sets) is never stated as a number and the value is hedged ('about 60%', 'roughly the same'). At most this is construct OTHER; I left it out under R4 rather than record a hedged value against an unstated denominator. (3) 'an article by the Gateway Pundit which made up 25% (23,000 shares) of the total of problematic content shared in that 4-day period' - a concentration-flavoured figure, but the denominator is problematic content only and there is no conc_group_pct (a single source's share of sources is never given), so R1 makes it unusable; it is also within-misinformation composition. (4) Findings 2, 3 and 5 (crossover of conservative/progressive sources across party keyword spaces; problematic sources outperforming mainstream in the DACA issue space in some weeks; few problematic sources among the top-20 most-retweeted tweets, e.g. 'the two tweets flagged as problematic in the Republican space in March') are reported only qualitatively or as figures (Figures 5.2-5.9) with no extractable percentages in the text. (5) Third-party figures (Silverman 2016 on Facebook, Bovet and Makse 2019, ComScore 2019 top-50 web properties, 'more than 40% of patients...' does not appear here) are cited from elsewhere and excluded by R8.

rob.design: Digital-methods study of 'political Twitter': curated keyword/hashtag queries for two parties, two candidates and three social issues (Table 5.1), captured with DMI-TCAT for 2-23 March 2020 and 24 December 2020-4 January 2021 and with 4CAT for 10-22 March 2021; close to 3 million tweets containing a news link captured, ~1 million shared media links analysed (no per-period denominators). Source veracity by domain list only: an author-built 'expert list' aggregating AllSides, Media Bias/Fact Check, 'the Chart' and NewsGuard, self-described as 'rough', with no reliability statistics and no per-source audit in the chapter. Top-20 most active users coded for authenticity (real/fake/bot/locked-suspended, categories adopted from SparkToro) and for partisanship (two authors labelled independently, disagreements resolved to 'unknown'); no kappa reported. Top-20 most retweeted tweets coded problematic if any linked source was on the problematic list. Sub-analyses rest on very small samples (top 20 users; issue spaces where 'one article can quickly spike engagement'), and the three waves differ in length (3 weeks vs ~12 days) and collection software. Data deposited at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/QIJQ3X.
